passages.t: The charge against the unfaithful mother
passages.happening:
The chapter begins with the names reversed: the children are to give their brothers and sisters back the names of belonging: God's people, and loved (verse 1). Then the LORD speaks as a wronged husband in a court of law. ‘Rebuke your mother, rebuke her, for she is not My wife, and I am not her husband’ (verse 2). Let her put away her adultery.

If she will not, he will strip her and make her like a desert, a parched land where she dies of thirst (verse 3). He will have no compassion on her children, because their mother has been unfaithful (verses 4-5). She said she would go after her lovers, because they give her bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 told the story of Hosea's household. Chapter 2 tells the story it stood for. The speaker now is mostly the LORD. The unfaithful wife is Israel as a people, and her children are the Israelites themselves, so the lines between Hosea's family and God's people blur on purpose.

The chapter fits the good years of Jeroboam II, when Israel had harvests, silver and gold, festivals and trade, and many gave Baal the credit. Baal was the storm god of the Canaanite world, known from texts found at Ugarit on the Syrian coast, and he was believed to bring the rain that made crops grow. Ahab and Jezebel had promoted his worship at court a century earlier, and Elijah had opposed it on Mount Carmel in a contest over who sends rain. Jehu purged Baal's temple in Samaria, but Hosea shows that Baal worship, or a blend of it with the worship of the LORD, lived on among the people. Receipts found at Samaria from the eighth century include personal names built on Baal beside names built on the LORD's name.

The language is the language of the law court and of marriage in the ancient world. A husband could divorce an unfaithful wife and send her away without what he owed her, and public stripping as a sign of disgrace was known. Hosea uses that world's language to make the weight of covenant betrayal felt.
passages.later: Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel was over who sends rain (1 Kings 18). Jeremiah and Ezekiel used the same picture of shaming as the judgment that falls on a city (Jeremiah 13:26; Ezekiel 16:37-39).
passages.hard:
How should the harsh images of stripping and exposure be read, here in verse 3 and again in verse 10?

Many readers find these lines painful, and readers who have known abuse may find them very hard. Several things help in reading them honestly. The chapter is a picture of a nation. The wife is Israel as a people, her lovers are Baal and the foreign powers she trusted, and the stripping describes what invasion and famine would do to the land, left bare like a desert. The images come from the legal customs of the ancient world, in which public shaming of an unfaithful wife was known, and the prophets used their culture's language to make the seriousness of betrayal felt. And the chapter does not stop there. Its turning point is the wilderness, where God speaks tenderly and makes a new covenant.

Scholars weigh the problem differently. Some, many feminist interpreters among them, argue that the picture, whatever its purpose, has shaped harmful attitudes and must be read critically. Others stress that it describes God's judgment on a nation and never permits any husband to treat a wife this way. Both agree that using this passage to justify the mistreatment of women is a grave misuse.

So it must be said plainly. This is a prophetic picture of God and a nation. It gives no warrant for any man to shame, strip, threaten or harm a wife, or anyone, and no one may use it to say that a woman deserves to be hurt.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Israel gave the credit for her bread and wool to the gods she thought were in charge of the rain. Ask what you credit for the good things you have. And if these verses are hard to read, it is right to say so to God, as the prophets themselves did.

passages.t: Her way blocked, and the gifts taken back
passages.happening:
‘Therefore, behold, I will hedge up her path with thorns’ (verse 6). She will chase her lovers and not catch them. Then she will say she will go back to her first husband, because she was better off then (verse 7). She does not acknowledge that ‘it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil’ (verse 8), and the silver and gold that were made into Baal's images.

So God will take back his grain and new wine in their seasons, and his wool and linen (verse 9). He will put an end to her celebrations, her feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths (verse 11). He will turn her vines and fig trees, which she calls her lovers' wages, into a thicket for wild animals (verse 12). He will punish her for the days she burned incense to the Baals and went after her lovers. ‘But Me she forgot,’ declares the LORD (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built on three therefores (verses 6, 9 and 14). Each follows a charge and says what God will do. The first two are acts of judgment: he blocks her way with thorns, and he takes back his gifts. A first hearer would expect the third to be the harshest of all.

Grain, new wine and oil were the three staple crops of the land, and with wool and linen they were the stuff of daily life. Hosea insists that they came from the LORD all along. A husband in Israel was obliged to provide for his wife, and here God withdraws what he gave. Israel's sin is not that she wanted good things. It is that she did not know who gave them, and chased the gifts instead of the giver.

The threat that God would take back the harvest and turn the vineyards to thicket came true in the Assyrian invasions of the 730s BC and the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. Blocking her way is also mercy. God hedges her in so that she will say she wants to go home.
passages.later: The law named what a husband owed a wife: food, clothing and marital rights (Exodus 21:10). Moses had warned Israel that when they ate and were satisfied they must not forget the LORD, ‘who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery’ (Deuteronomy 8:14).
passages.asks: Verse 7 shows someone who wants to go back only because she was better off before. Ask whether you return to God for his sake or only for what he gives. And ask where a blocked path in your own life might be a mercy.

passages.t: Wooed in the wilderness, and betrothed forever
passages.happening:
Then comes the third therefore, and it is a surprise. ‘Therefore, behold, I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly’ (verse 14). He will give back her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor ‘into a gateway of hope’ (verse 15), and she will answer as she did when she came up out of Egypt.

In that day she will call him her husband, no longer her master, and God will remove the names of the Baals from her lips (verses 16-17). He will make a covenant for his people with the animals, abolish bow and sword, and let them lie down in safety (verse 18). ‘So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion. And I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will know the LORD’ (verses 19-20).

On that day God will answer the heavens, the heavens the earth, and the earth the grain and wine and oil, and they will answer Jezreel (verses 21-22). He will sow her as his own in the land, have compassion on No Compassion, and say to Not My People that they are his people, and they will say that he is their God (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The wilderness was where Israel had first followed the LORD after the exodus, in the days of her youth. God does not drag her back. He leads her to the place where it began and speaks to her heart. The Valley of Achor was near Jericho, where Achan was put to death for taking forbidden plunder (Joshua 7). Its name means trouble. The valley of trouble becomes a door of hope.

The word baal meant master, owner or husband in ordinary speech, so an Israelite could call the LORD baal, master, without meaning anything pagan. Verse 16 ends the confusion. She will call him ishi, husband, a word for a personal partner, not baali, master or owner. Even the word will be gone.

To betroth was to pledge a woman in marriage by paying the bride price. The word comes three times, as if God will begin the marriage again rather than patch it up. And God pays the price himself, in righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion and faithfulness. Loving devotion is hesed, the loyal love Israel lacks. God brings it himself. The chapter ends with the whole creation answering, and with all three children's names from chapter 1 reversed.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 23 with 1:10 to show God calling those who were not his people: ‘As He says in Hosea’ (Romans 9:25). Peter does the same for believers scattered abroad: ‘once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy’ (1 Peter 2:10).
passages.asks: God speaks tenderly in the wilderness. Ask whether a hard season has ever become a place where you heard him more clearly. And ask what it means to you that he calls himself a husband and not a master.
